newsitem.title: FRANCE: 34 hurt in blaze in Channel Tunnel freight train.
newsitem.headline: 34 hurt in blaze in Channel Tunnel freight train.

text.p: Thirty-four people were injured, two seriously, in a fire aboard a train carrying trucks through the Channel Tunnel, officials said early on Tuesday.
It was the worst accident since the undersea rail link between France and Britain opened two years ago.
A total of eight people were taken to hospital. The rest were given treatment for varying degrees of smoke inhalation.

Fire-fighters from France and Britain in special breathing gear brought the fire under control deep inside the tunnel early on Tuesday but it was still smouldering more than six hours after starting in a truck carrying a load of polystyrene.
The fire, and choking toxic fumes, forced closure of the 51-km (32-mile) tunnel.

Franco-British operator Eurotunnel SA Plc hoped to reopen the tunnel during the day but cancelled early trains between Paris, Brussels and London as well as suspending its shuttle service for trucks and cars between France's Calais and Folkstone on the British side.

"Thirty-four people were affected, both passengers and train staff. The two most seriously injured were taken by helicopter to Lille hospital (near Calais) but their lives are not in danger," said Jean-Pascal Cogez, deputy prefect in Calais.
"Six passengers were hospitalised in Calais and 26 others were placed under medical surveillance after inhaling smoke," he told Reuters.
All the truck drivers who were in the freight shuttle were evacuated either on a train or by ambulance from the tunnel. The first fire-fighters arrived within about 10 minutes.

The cause of the fire, which spread to three other trucks in the train, was unknown. A legal probe would be opened in France into the blaze, the latest in a series of woes for the tunnel, dogged by cost over-runs and fierce competition from ferries.

The freight shuttle train, used to transport trucks and their drivers, was halted and evacuated between 9 and 10 p.m. (same GMT). It was believed to be about 12 miles (19 km) from the French end of the tunnel.
Francois Borel, a spokeswoman for Eurotunnel, said: "The fire is under control but the train is still blocked in the tunnel."

"We hope to open the tunnel sometime later on Tuesday," he said. When reopened, the tunnel would be reduced to a single track from its normal twin tracks running north and south. "That's the situation we have when we're carrying out maintenance on the tunnel," he said.
The fire broke out towards the back of the 730 metre (yard) long train, which has locomotives at both front and back and can carry up to 28 large trucks, a Eurotunnel spokeswoman said in London.
"It is the first time the tunnel has been closed for an emergency. We have had safety drills in the past but this is the first real event," she said.
The passengers and crew were evacuated from the northbound tunnel to a central service shaft and then transported via another shuttle train back to France via the southbound tunnel.
More than 20 fire appliances gathered at the British end of the tunnel near Folkestone and up to six French fire engines were reported at Calais.
Crews in breathing gear were reported to be rotating in shifts to tackle the dense smoke and searing heat generated by the fire in the narrow confines of the tunnel.
Firefighters used a freshwater main running the length of the tunnel to douse the flames.
